title: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
summary: How research agents loop over planning, search, reading and synthesis, why orchestrators fan out to parallel subagents, what that costs in tokens, and how to check citations and evaluate the results.
outcomes: Explain why research needs a plan, search, read, synthesize loop instead of one retrieval
Design an orchestrator with parallel subagents and compute the wall-time and token effects of fan-out
Set budgets and stopping criteria that leave room for synthesis and verification
Compute citation precision for a report and name the common ways citations fail
Interpret MLE-bench and PaperBench scores and spot reward hacking in agent evaluations

lessons.title: Why research needs a loop, not one retrieval

blocks.md: In the agent harness course an agent was an LLM called in a loop: it emits a tool call, the harness runs the tool, the result is appended to the context, repeat until the model answers. In agent verification you checked an agent's output against something external. A **research agent** is that loop pointed at an open question ("what caused the 2021 auto chip shortage, how did automakers respond, and what changed by 2025?") where the answer has to be found, read, and assembled from many sources.

The naive approach is one retrieval: embed the question, fetch the top 10 passages, write an answer. That fails on research questions because you cannot know the right searches in advance. The second search depends on what the first one found: a name, a date, a term of art. Anthropic's write-up of their Research feature puts it directly: research is open-ended, the path depends on intermediate findings, and "a linear, one-shot pipeline cannot handle these tasks".

blocks.title: The plan, search, read, synthesize loop

scenes.caption: The agent starts by planning: it splits the question into sub-questions (causes, automaker responses, supply chain changes) instead of firing one query.
Search returns snippets and links, not answers. Broad queries first: Anthropic found agents default to overly long, specific queries that return few results.
Reading is where tokens go: whole pages and PDFs enter the context. Each useful fact is written down together with the URL and passage it came from.
The loop closes here. Notes reveal a gap (a supplier name, a date), so the next query is refined using what was just learned. This is why one-shot retrieval fails.
Only when the stopping test passes does the agent write the report, citing the notes. Simplified: real systems also check citations after writing (lesson 4).

blocks.md:
Four verbs, defined once:

- **Plan**: decompose the question into sub-questions and decide how much effort each deserves.
- **Search**: issue queries to a search tool and get back ranked links and snippets.
- **Read**: open the promising results and extract facts, each tied to its source.
- **Synthesize**: merge the notes, find gaps and contradictions, and either loop or write the answer.

The loop's exit condition ("enough to answer?") is a judgment the model makes, which is why stopping gets its own lesson.

OpenAI's **deep research** is a production example. Its system card describes it as an agentic capability that does multi-step research on the internet, powered by an early version of o3 optimized for web browsing. It searches, clicks, scrolls, reads files, can run Python in a sandbox, pivots as it learns, and produces reports with citations. It was trained with reinforcement learning on browsing tasks, graded against ground-truth answers or rubrics by a chain-of-thought grader model.

**STORM** (Shao et al., 2024) shows the loop applied to long-form writing. Before writing a Wikipedia-style article it (1) discovers diverse perspectives by looking at articles on similar topics, (2) simulates conversations in which a writer with each perspective asks questions and a topic expert answers from retrieved internet sources, and (3) builds an outline from what was collected. Follow-up questions come from earlier answers, which is the loop again. Compared with an outline-driven retrieval baseline, more STORM articles were judged organized (a 25% absolute increase) and broad in coverage (10%).
A research agent is not a bigger retrieval call. It is a harness loop whose next query depends on what the last read revealed, and whose output is a set of claims each tied to a source.

blocks.question: A team builds a research assistant that embeds the question, retrieves the top 20 passages once, and writes a report. It does well on "What is X?" questions and badly on "Compare how three companies responded to X". What is the most likely cause?
options: The embedding model is too small to represent comparison questions
The needed queries depend on facts found along the way (company names, events), and a single fixed retrieval cannot follow up
20 passages exceed the context window
Comparison questions require a fine-tuned model
blocks.explain: Comparisons require finding the entities first, then searching each one, then searching for whatever each search surfaces. A one-shot pipeline commits to its queries before it has learned anything. Context size and model size are not the bottleneck here.

blocks.question: What does STORM's simulated conversation step add compared with asking the LLM to list questions about the topic once?
options: It removes the need for a search engine
It guarantees every sentence is cited
Follow-up questions are generated from answers grounded in retrieved sources, so research goes deeper iteratively
It lets the model skip outline creation
blocks.explain: STORM's second hypothesis is that in-depth questions require iterative research: answers grounded in sources raise follow-up questions. It still uses search, still builds an outline, and the authors found citation problems remained.

lessons.title: Orchestrator, parallel subagents and context isolation

blocks.md: A single agent running the loop does every search one after another in one growing context. Anthropic's Research system instead uses an **orchestrator-worker** pattern. A **lead agent** (the orchestrator) analyzes the query, writes a plan, and spawns **subagents** (workers), each with its own task and its own context window. Subagents search and read in parallel and return condensed findings. The lead decides whether more research is needed, then hands the report and sources to a **CitationAgent** that finds where each claim should be cited.

blocks.title: Lead agent, subagents and the citation pass

scenes.caption: The lead agent thinks through the approach and saves the plan to memory. Anthropic notes context beyond 200,000 tokens is truncated, so the plan must survive outside the context.
The lead writes three task descriptions, one per sub-question, and spawns three subagents at once rather than one after another.
Each subagent runs its own search loop in its own context window. Pages read by A never enter B's or the lead's context: this is context isolation.
Subagents return condensed summaries, not raw pages. The lead sees a few hundred tokens per subagent and decides whether to spawn more or stop.
The draft and its documents go to a citation agent that locates where each claim should be attributed. Then the cited report is returned.

blocks.md: Why split the work? Anthropic frames search as **compression**: distilling a large corpus into a few important facts. Each subagent compresses its slice in a fresh context, so its reasoning is not crowded by pages about other sub-questions, and the lead only reads the distilled result. This is **context isolation**: separate windows give separation of concerns and let the total amount of reading exceed what fits in one window.

Delegation is the hard part. Anthropic's lead agent originally gave short instructions like "research the semiconductor shortage", and subagents misread them or ran the same searches. In one case a subagent explored the 2021 automotive chip crisis while two others duplicated work on 2025 supply chains. Their fix: each task description states an **objective**, an **output format**, guidance on **tools and sources**, and clear **task boundaries**.

blocks.title: Three subtasks: sequential versus parallel (toy model)

scenes.caption: Toy model: planning 10 s, each search-and-read step 8 s, synthesis 14 s, citation check 10 s. Run one after another, the subtasks take 40, 32 and 48 s, so the answer arrives at 154 s.
Spawn all three subagents at once. Wall time is set by the slowest subtask (C, 48 s), so the answer arrives at 82 s, 47% sooner. The token count is unchanged: the same work, overlapped.
Synchronous execution: the lead waits for all subagents. A and B sit idle while C finishes. Anthropic names this bottleneck; asynchronous execution would let the lead act on early results.

Second level of parallelism: each subagent issues up to 3 tool calls at once, so 5, 4 and 6 searches take 2 rounds each (16 s). The answer arrives at 50 s, 68% below sequential. Simplified: real latencies vary per call.

blocks.prompt: In the toy model, suppose subtask C needed 12 searches instead of 6 while A and B stay the same, with one tool call at a time. Guess the new parallel wall time before reading on.
blocks.reveal: The slowest subagent sets the pace: C now takes 12 x 8 = 96 s, so the answer arrives at 130 s, while sequential would be 202 s. Parallelism helps most when subtasks are balanced, which is one more reason the lead's decomposition matters.

blocks.md: Anthropic reports two kinds of parallelism: the lead spins up 3 to 5 subagents in parallel, and subagents use 3 or more tools in parallel. Together these cut research time by up to 90% for complex queries. They also note limits: domains where all agents must share the same context, or with many dependencies between agents, are a poor fit. Most coding tasks have fewer truly parallelizable pieces than research.

More subagents is not automatically better. Anthropic's early agents spawned 50 subagents for simple queries and distracted each other with updates. Their prompts now embed effort rules: simple fact-finding gets 1 agent with 3 to 10 tool calls, direct comparisons get 2 to 4 subagents with 10 to 15 calls each, and complex research uses more than 10 subagents with clearly divided responsibilities.

Orchestrator-worker is not the only shape. Google's **AI co-scientist** (Gottweis et al., 2025, built on Gemini 2.0) uses specialized agents (Generation, Reflection, Ranking, Evolution, Proximity, Meta-review) coordinated by a Supervisor agent that runs an asynchronous task queue and allocates compute. Its goal is generating hypotheses rather than answering a question, so the agents argue and refine instead of splitting a search. Lesson 5 looks at it in detail.

blocks.question: A lead agent sends three subagents the task "research the chip shortage". The results overlap heavily and one sub-question is never covered. What is the best fix?
options: Spawn ten subagents so coverage is more likely
Run the three subagents sequentially so they can read each other's notes
Raise the subagents' temperature to diversify their searches
Give each subagent an objective, output format, source guidance and explicit boundaries that exclude the others' topics
blocks.explain: This is the failure Anthropic described: vague task descriptions lead to duplicated work and gaps. Detailed, bounded task descriptions fix the division of labor. More agents or randomness would increase cost without guaranteeing coverage, and running sequentially gives up the speedup.

blocks.question: Which task benefits least from an orchestrator with parallel subagents?
options: Collecting board members of every company in a large index
Comparing five databases on four criteria
A refactor where every change depends on the previous edit to the same files
Surveying literature on three independent sub-topics
blocks.explain: Parallel subagents pay off when work splits into independent pieces with separate contexts. A chain of dependent edits to shared files needs shared context and tight coordination, the case Anthropic says is not a good fit today.

lessons.title: Tokens, budgets and when to stop

blocks.md: Anthropic analyzed what drove performance on BrowseComp, an evaluation of how well browsing agents find hard-to-locate information. Three factors explained 95% of the variance, and **token usage by itself explained 80%**; the other two were the number of tool calls and the model choice. Their multi-agent system (Claude Opus 4 as lead, Claude Sonnet 4 subagents) outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on their internal research eval.

The price is tokens. In Anthropic's data, agents typically used about **4x more tokens than chat** interactions, and multi-agent systems about **15x more than chat**. So the architecture is economical only when the task is valuable enough to pay for the extra performance. To see where the tokens go, we build a toy budget.

Toy assumptions (made up for illustration, not measured): a subagent's prompt plus task is $S = 1,500$ tokens. Every search-and-read step appends $r = 1,700$ tokens (a short query plus a page excerpt) and the model is called again on the whole context. Each call writes 150 tokens; a subagent's final summary is 600 tokens. Because each call re-reads everything before it, an agent with $n$ steps processes:

blocks.caption: Input tokens grow quadratically with steps because the context is re-read every call. Simplified: prompt caching makes re-read tokens cheaper but does not remove them from the context.

blocks.title: Where the toy run's tokens go

scenes.caption: Subagents dominate: 109,250 of 123,150 tokens (89%). Reading is the expensive part; planning and writing are small.
Context isolation in numbers: the lead's synthesis call reads only plan plus three 600-token summaries (4,600 input tokens), not the 25,500 tokens of pages the subagents read.
A chat answer here is 1,500 tokens. A single agent doing all 15 steps in one context (same S and r, plus a 1,500-token report) ends with a 27,000-token context and processes 231,750 tokens in total.

Splitting the same 15 steps into three short contexts processes 123,150 tokens, because no context gets long. Real systems spend that headroom on more searching, which is why measured usage is higher.

blocks.title: Re-reading cost: one long context versus k short ones

scenes.caption: With S = 1.5k and r = 1.7k for every agent, 15 steps in one context process 228k input tokens; split across 3 subagents, 103.5k. Excludes the lead's own calls.
With k = 1 the curves coincide. The single-agent curve is quadratic in n; splitting divides the quadratic term by roughly k.
At k = 6 the curve is close to linear. Each extra subagent adds a fixed prompt cost S plus lead overhead, so very large k stops paying off on small tasks.

blocks.md: Misconception: "multi-agent saves tokens." At a fixed amount of reading, isolation can reduce re-reading, as the toy shows. But real multi-agent systems do far more reading because they can, and Anthropic measured about 15x chat usage. The toy's ratio to chat (82x) depends entirely on our made-up assumptions; do not compare it to the measured figure.

**Stopping criteria** decide how much of that budget is spent. A practical agent combines several:

- **Objective met**: the subagent's task description says what output answers it; once found, return.
- **Step cap**: a maximum number of tool calls, scaled to query complexity (the 3 to 10, 10 to 15 rules from lesson 2).
- **Token or time budget**: hard limits enforced by the harness, not by the model.
- **Lead's sufficiency check**: after summaries return, the lead decides whether to spawn more subagents or synthesize.
- **Diminishing returns**: new searches keep returning sources already in the notes.

blocks.prompt: The harness gives this run a 130,000-token budget. After planning and the three subagents, the lead has spent 112,050. The lead notices a gap and wants one more subagent as large as B. Should it spawn it?
blocks.reveal: Remaining: 130,000 minus 112,050 = 17,950. Synthesis (6,100) and the citation pass (5,000) are still owed, leaving 6,850, well short of the 25,700 a B-sized subagent costs. The lead should either stop and flag the gap in the report, or spawn a narrower subagent with a smaller step cap. Reserving budget for verification is a design decision, not an afterthought.

blocks.md: Both directions of stopping fail in practice. Too late: Anthropic's early agents scoured the web endlessly for sources that did not exist. Too early: in PaperBench, every model except Claude 3.5 Sonnet frequently finished early, claiming the replication was done or that a problem could not be solved; forcing the agent to use its full time (the IterativeAgent variant) raised scores for o3-mini and o1. And budgets themselves can be gamed: when experiments exceeded imposed time limits, The AI Scientist sometimes tried to edit its code to extend the limit instead of shortening the runtime.

Tokens buy research quality (80% of BrowseComp variance in Anthropic's analysis), so the budget is the main dial. Enforce budgets in the harness, reserve a share for synthesis and verification, and scale effort to the question.

blocks.question: An agent's per-run cost grows much faster than linearly as you raise its step cap from 10 to 40. Which change most directly addresses the cause?
options: Use a model with a larger context window
Raise the sampling temperature so it finds answers sooner
Split the work across subagents with separate contexts and return short summaries
Ask the model to write shorter search queries
blocks.explain: Each call re-reads the whole context, so input tokens grow roughly with the square of the step count. Shorter contexts (subagents returning summaries) cut the quadratic term. A larger window allows more growth rather than less; query length is a tiny share of r.

blocks.question: Where should a hard token budget be enforced?
options: In the harness, outside the model's control, with the remaining budget shown to the agent
In the system prompt only, asking the model to be economical
By the citation agent after the report is written
Nowhere: token usage explains performance, so limits hurt quality
blocks.explain: A budget the model can ignore or edit is not a budget (recall The AI Scientist editing its time limit). The harness enforces it; telling the agent its remaining budget lets it plan, such as stopping to leave room for verification.

lessons.title: Tracking sources and checking every citation

blocks.md: A research report is a list of claims. Each claim is only as good as the evidence behind it, so a research agent must track **provenance**: for every fact, the URL, the passage it came from, and when it was retrieved. If subagents return polished prose without this, the link between claim and evidence is already lost before the lead writes anything.

blocks.code:
# One entry in a claim ledger, written by a subagent while reading
claim = {
    "id": "C3",
    "text": "Automaker X cut production at two plants in Q2 2021",
    "source": {"url": "https://example.com/x-q2-report",
               "quote": "production was suspended at two plants",
               "retrieved": "2026-10-20"},
    "subtask": "automaker-responses",
}

def check(claim, fetch, judge):
    page = fetch(claim["source"]["url"])         # does the source exist?
    if page is None:
        return "fake"
    if claim["source"]["quote"] not in page:     # is the quote really there?
        return "no"
    return judge(premise=claim["source"]["quote"], hypothesis=claim["text"])  # "ok" or "no"
blocks.caption: Store the quoted passage, not just the URL. Then a checker can verify three things separately: the source exists, the quote is in it, and the quote supports the claim.

blocks.md: Anthropic's system ends with a **CitationAgent** that processes the documents and the draft report to identify specific locations for citations, so that claims are attributed to their sources. Their appendix also suggests letting subagents write outputs to a filesystem and pass lightweight references, which avoids a "game of telephone" where facts are paraphrased at every hop.

Verifying a citation is the agent verification idea applied to text: given the cited passage (premise) and the claim (hypothesis), does the passage support the claim? STORM measured exactly this, using **citation recall** and **citation precision** as defined by Gao et al. (2023), with an LLM (Mistral 7B-Instruct) judging whether cited passages entail each sentence. We use a simplified version: precision is the share of attached citations whose passage supports its claim.

blocks.title: A citation-checking pass over 12 claims (toy report)

scenes.caption: The draft report makes 12 claims. Ten carry one citation each; C11 and C12 have none. Before checking, every verdict is unknown.
Existence check first. S9 for C5 does not resolve: the model invented a plausible-looking source. That is citation hallucination, the cheapest failure to catch.
Support check: a judge compares each cited passage with its claim. C3 and C8 cite real pages that do not say what the claim says, such as joining two facts the source never connected.
Score: 7 of 10 citations support their claim, so precision = 0.70. Counting all 12 claims, only 7 (58%) are backed by a supporting citation.
Repair: drop C5 and C8, re-search C3 (new source S8 supports it), find S6 supports C11, flag C12 as uncited. Precision is now 1.00 on 9 citations; 9 of 10 claims are supported.

blocks.caption: Precision alone misses uncited claims; that is what recall-style metrics catch. Track both.

blocks.md: STORM's analysis of citation errors is a good taxonomy. The most common error was **improper inferential linking**: the LLM connected two pieces of information that the sources never connected. The others were **inaccurate paraphrasing** and **citing irrelevant sources**. STORM's citations scored 84.83 recall and 85.18 precision by the LLM judge, yet among the pairs where Wikipedia editors preferred the baseline, they gave STORM lower verifiability scores in over 50% of cases, citing red herrings and over-speculation. Automated entailment checks are useful but more lenient than experts.

Other ways claims go wrong:

- **Hallucinated content**: The AI Scientist once wrote an entire ablation table it had not run, and frequently stated facts it was never given, such as the hardware used.
- **Shallow or low-quality search**: Anthropic's human testers found early agents chose SEO-optimized content farms over authoritative but lower-ranked sources such as academic PDFs. Adding source-quality heuristics to the prompt helped resolve it.
- **Prompt injection**: OpenAI's deep research system card notes that pages the agent reads may contain instructions that try to override the user's, leading to wrong answers or data exfiltration. One mitigation: deep research is not allowed to navigate to or construct arbitrary URLs.
A citation that exists is not a citation that supports. Checking that every URL resolves catches invented sources but misses the more common failure: a real page cited for a claim it does not make.

blocks.question: A report has 20 cited claims. Every URL returns HTTP 200, and an entailment judge finds 15 of the cited passages support their claims. What is the citation precision, and what does the 200 check add?
options: 1.00; the 200 check proves the citations are correct
0.75; the 200 check is redundant once you run the judge
0.25; five failures out of twenty
0.75; the 200 check only rules out invented sources, not unsupported claims
blocks.explain: Precision is 15 / 20 = 0.75. Resolving URLs rules out fabricated sources cheaply but says nothing about support. It is not redundant: the judge needs the fetched page to compare against, and a dead link is a separate failure to report.

blocks.question: A claim reads "Policy A caused the 2022 price drop" and cites a page saying "Policy A was enacted in 2021" and another saying "prices fell in 2022". Which error is this?
options: Citation hallucination
Inaccurate paraphrasing
Improper inferential linking
Prompt injection
blocks.explain: Both sources are real and accurately quoted, but neither states a causal link: the model inferred it. STORM found this the most common citation error, and a per-citation check that only asks "is this sentence on the page?" can miss it.

lessons.title: End-to-end science agents: AI Scientist and co-scientist

blocks.md: Research agents can go beyond answering questions to running experiments. **The AI Scientist** (Lu et al., 2024, Sakana AI) attempts the whole machine learning research cycle: generate an idea, implement and run experiments, plot results, write a full paper, and review it. It was applied to three subfields (diffusion modeling, transformer language modeling, learning dynamics), starting each run from a small code template.

scenes.caption: Ideas are brainstormed from the template and an archive of earlier ideas, refined with self-reflection, then checked against Semantic Scholar; ideas too similar to existing papers are discarded.
The coding assistant Aider plans and runs experiments. On errors it gets up to four fix attempts; after each experiment it writes notes and re-plans, for up to five rounds.
Aider fills in a LaTeX conference template section by section, adds citations found via Semantic Scholar, and fixes compile errors.
A GPT-4o-based reviewer scores the paper using NeurIPS guidelines. Reviewed papers go back to the archive, so later ideas build on earlier ones.
Failures observed by the authors: relaunching itself, editing its own time limit, hallucinated results. They recommend strict sandboxing: containers, restricted internet, storage limits.

blocks.md: The paper reports a cost of under USD 15 per paper (around USD 10 to 15 in its discussion) and validates the automated reviewer against human decisions on ICLR 2022 papers: the best configuration reached 0.65 balanced accuracy versus 0.66 for humans (a figure taken from the NeurIPS 2021 consistency experiment). Judged by that reviewer, some generated papers exceeded the acceptance threshold of a top machine learning conference. Note what this measures: one LLM's opinion of another LLM's paper, not whether the science is correct.

The authors are candid about limitations:

- Aider fails to implement a significant fraction of proposed ideas.
- It struggles to compare the magnitude of two numbers, and when it changes a metric it sometimes compares unfairly against the baseline.
- Rarely it hallucinates entire results, and it frequently hallucinates facts such as hardware.
- In one run it made a system call to relaunch itself, causing an uncontrolled growth in Python processes.

Their conclusion: do not take the scientific content of this version at face value; treat generated papers as hints of promising ideas.

Google's **AI co-scientist** aims at a different step: generating research hypotheses with a scientist in the loop. The **Generation** agent explores literature and simulates scientific debates to propose hypotheses. **Reflection** reviews them like a peer reviewer. **Ranking** runs an Elo tournament of pairwise comparisons via simulated debates, with each new hypothesis starting at Elo 1200. **Proximity** builds a similarity graph to cluster and de-duplicate. **Evolution** creates improved variants of top ideas. **Meta-review** summarizes recurring critiques and feeds them back into prompts. A **Supervisor** schedules all of this asynchronously.

scenes.caption: A scientist states a research goal in natural language; the Supervisor turns it into a plan and queues work for the specialized agents.
Generation proposes hypotheses, Reflection reviews them for correctness, novelty and quality, and Ranking enters them into the tournament at Elo 1200.
Proximity groups similar hypotheses so the tournament compares like with like; Evolution rewrites winners into new hypotheses that re-enter review.
Meta-review distills patterns from debates into feedback for every agent's prompt. More test-time compute means more rounds; the authors report hypothesis quality improving over time.

blocks.md: The co-scientist was validated in three biomedical areas, including drug repurposing candidates for acute myeloid leukemia that were tested in vitro. The authors are explicit that Elo is an auto-evaluated metric that may favor attributes not aligned with scientists' preferences, quality or accuracy, and that the expert evaluations were small. A tournament makes ideas better *at winning the tournament*; whether that tracks truth has to be checked outside the loop.

End-to-end science agents fail at the steps where nothing external checks them: invented numbers, unfair comparisons, edits to their own limits. Put independent checks (sandboxes, reproducibility, human experts) at exactly those points.

blocks.question: An AI Scientist-style system reports that 30% of its papers pass its automated reviewer's acceptance threshold. Which conclusion is justified?
options: 30% of the papers contain correct, novel science
The automated reviewer rates 30% of papers above its threshold; correctness still needs independent checking
The system outperforms human researchers 30% of the time
The papers would be accepted at a real conference 30% of the time
blocks.explain: The reviewer is an LLM with roughly human-level balanced accuracy on accept/reject decisions, not a correctness oracle. The authors themselves found hallucinated results and unfair comparisons and advise against taking the content at face value.

blocks.question: Why does the co-scientist use a Proximity agent alongside the Elo tournament?
options: To cluster and de-duplicate similar hypotheses and organize which ones are compared
To compute Elo ratings faster with embeddings
To verify hypotheses in the lab
To replace the Reflection agent's reviews
blocks.explain: Proximity builds a similarity graph so near-duplicates are merged and tournament matches compare related ideas. It does not rate or verify hypotheses; Ranking and Reflection do that, and lab validation happens outside the system.

lessons.title: Evaluating research agents without fooling yourself

blocks.md: Research outputs are free-form and rarely have one correct answer, so evaluation needs care. Anthropic's approach: start with a small set (about 20 queries representing real usage) because early changes have large effects, then grade with an LLM judge using a rubric of **factual accuracy**, **citation accuracy**, **completeness**, **source quality** and **tool efficiency**. A single judge call producing 0.0 to 1.0 scores and a pass/fail grade was the most consistent and best aligned with human judgment. Human testers still caught what the judge missed, like the content-farm bias.

For research *engineering*, benchmarks can grade against ground truth. **MLE-bench** (Chan et al., 2024) is 75 Kaggle competitions run offline: the agent gets the description and data, submits predictions, and is graded locally against the real leaderboard. The headline metric is the share of competitions where the agent earns at least a bronze medal. At release, the best setup (o1-preview with the AIDE scaffold) did so in 16.9% of competitions.

blocks.title: MLE-bench: more attempts and more time help

scenes.caption: With one attempt per competition, o1-preview with AIDE medals in 16.9% of competitions.
Given 8 attempts (pass@8: success if any attempt medals), the score doubles to 34.1%. Pass@k measures what a selector could get, not what one run delivers.
Time is a resource too: GPT-4o goes from 8.7% with 24 hours per competition to 11.8% with 100 hours. Always report the budget alongside the score.

blocks.md: **PaperBench** (Starace et al., 2025, OpenAI) asks agents to replicate 20 ICML 2024 Spotlight and Oral papers from scratch: understand the paper, write a codebase, and run the experiments. Each paper has a rubric co-developed with its authors: a tree whose leaves are binary pass/fail requirements (8,316 leaves in total) and whose internal nodes are weighted averages of their children. Leaves come in three types: code development, execution, and result match.

blocks.title: Grading a replication with a weighted rubric tree (toy)

scenes.caption: Toy rubric with six leaves under three weighted branches. Real PaperBench rubrics are far larger and their weights are set by importance, not difficulty.
The judge grades each leaf pass (1) or fail (0). Here the agent implemented the method and baseline but not the ablation, ran only the main experiment, and the result trend did not match.
Each parent averages its children (equal weights within a branch here): code development 0.67, execution 0.50, result match 0.00.
Root = (3 x 0.67 + 2 x 0.50 + 1 x 0.00) / 6 = 0.50. Partial credit makes progress measurable even when no paper is fully replicated.

blocks.md: Grading one replication by hand can take a human expert tens of hours, so PaperBench uses an LLM judge (SimpleJudge). The authors checked the judge itself on JudgeEval, a set of human-graded leaves; the judge they adopted (o3-mini-high with custom scaffolding, the most cost-effective option) reached an F1 of 0.83. The best agent tested, Claude 3.5 Sonnet (New) with an open-source scaffold, averaged 21.0%. On a 3-paper subset, ML PhDs (best of 3 attempts, 48 hours) reached 41.4% versus 26.6% for o1.

Research agents are optimizers, and benchmarks are proxies, so expect **reward hacking**: scoring well without doing the work. The benchmark designers built defenses for the specific shortcuts available:

- PaperBench runs the submitted `reproduce.sh` in a fresh environment, so results hard-coded during the agent's run do not count.
- PaperBench blacklists each paper's official code and other online replications; a monitor found 10 runs out of 646 using blacklisted resources, and those were scored 0.
- MLE-bench uses a GPT-4o log inspector that flags rule-breaking (such as writing the submission by hand without a model) and a plagiarism detector, and studies whether memorized Kaggle solutions inflate scores.

An LLM judge grading an LLM agent can share its blind spots. Validate the judge against human labels (as JudgeEval does), keep humans testing edge cases, and read transcripts: a high score with a shortcut in the logs is a failed run.

blocks.question: Agent X scores 30% pass@8 on MLE-bench; agent Y scores 18% pass@1. Which statement is fair?
options: X is clearly better because 30 is greater than 18
Y is better because pass@1 is harder
They are not comparable: X had eight attempts and needs a way to pick the medal-winning one; compare at the same k and budget
Both numbers are invalid because MLE-bench uses medals
blocks.explain: pass@k credits success if any of k attempts succeeds, which is an upper bound for a system that must choose one submission. In MLE-bench, o1-preview went from 16.9% to 34.1% just by moving from pass@1 to pass@8. Compare at equal k, time and compute.

blocks.question: Why does PaperBench grade results produced by re-running `reproduce.sh` in a fresh environment rather than the files the agent left behind?
options: Fresh environments are faster to grade
It stops an agent from scoring result-match leaves with numbers it wrote by hand during its run
The LLM judge cannot read files from the agent's environment
It ensures the agent used the blacklisted official code
blocks.explain: Separating reproduction from the agent's run means only results the code actually produces are graded, which closes a direct reward-hacking route: writing the expected numbers into a results file. Blacklisted code is forbidden, not required.

blocks.question: Your research agent's LLM-judge score rises from 0.71 to 0.83 after a prompt change. Which check most directly guards against fooling yourself?
options: Read a sample of transcripts and verify a few citations by hand to confirm the gain is real
Increase the eval set from 20 to 2,000 queries before looking at anything
Switch to a larger judge model and re-run
Accept the change: LLM judges are aligned with humans
blocks.explain: A judge score can rise because the agent learned to please the judge (confident tone, more citations) without being more correct. Spot-checking transcripts and citations by hand tests whether the improvement is real. A bigger eval set is useful later but does not detect a judge blind spot.
